ancient-trails.intro: At Fenglaoye Ancient Tea Garden, the proposal reconnects a tea factory, existing accommodation and a dispersed mountain landscape through a walking network. Reception, production, rest and bathing are assigned different degrees of architectural presence. More collective uses concentrate near accessible ground; smaller accommodation units occupy selected clearings. The design works from the relation between route and programme down to the assembly of a raised floor. It is a graduation design proposal, with environmental and operational performance still to be tested.

01: The layout begins with the places that already anchor the site. A public reception establishes arrival and orientation, while the route reconnects tea-making with the garden and stopping places. The intervention is distributed so that movement reveals a sequence of activities rather than an isolated destination.

Public and private movement are differentiated within that network. Collective facilities need to be easy to find and service; accommodation needs a degree of separation from the walking route. Changes in alignment and threshold allow visitors to remain connected to the landscape without making every room part of a public promenade. The network drawing should be read through these branches and relationships.
02: Construction changes with the ground. The studies use raised floors, point foundations, timber members and bracing to organise small units without a continuous ground slab. Modular components and replaceable connections are proposed to make assembly and later repair more manageable along the route.

The architectural detail is tied to logistics. A compact footprint still requires a way to bring materials in, install foundations and maintain services. The proposal therefore concentrates more demanding shared uses where access is less constrained. Root zones, slope stability, installation methods and the treatment cycle for bathing facilities remain technical questions for a subsequent stage.

ancient-trails.note: The research essay examines why production and access might sustain the trail. These drawings show the proposed distribution of facilities, the separation of routes and the construction approach chosen to test that argument.

first-teaching-building.intro: This commission renews the third floor of Tsinghua’s First Teaching Building through restrained changes to rooms, surfaces and building services. The 30 January 2026 proposal covers 682 m²: two 96-seat classrooms, a multifunctional classroom, circulation and a teachers’ lounge. The design retains the inherited structure, proportions and window openings. Its main work is coordination—making acoustic treatment, lighting, ventilation, equipment and furniture support contemporary teaching within the building’s existing order. The images show a design stage, not completed construction.

01: The two large classrooms remain the principal teaching rooms, while the multifunctional room provides another scale of occupation between them. The plan places their entrances along the shared circulation spine and retains a separate teachers’ lounge. The programme combines fixed-capacity teaching with a room that can change between lecture, review, screening and group activity.

The original building’s 1952 order guides the extent of alteration. Structure and openings remain the primary frame; new work is concentrated in finishes, equipment and the organisation of use. Keeping this hierarchy clear helps distinguish the inherited building from elements expected to change again as teaching methods evolve.
02: The corridor is treated as an occupied part of the floor. Seating and power points support short work sessions and conversations between classes. Retained timber doors remain visible within a restrained palette of pale wall surfaces and differentiated flooring. The design seeks continuity through material and alignment rather than a new decorative identity.

Wood-wool acoustic panels follow the ceiling order. Lighting and supply/return air outlets are coordinated at their edges, while heating is integrated with the lower wall and grilles. These details bring services into the same spatial composition as the doors, seating and circulation. Final service sizing, acoustic performance and maintenance access require coordination during detailed design.
03: The classrooms combine teaching equipment with layouts suited to their different capacities. The multifunctional room uses adaptable furniture and presentation surfaces to accommodate several arrangements. Its flexibility comes from changing occupation within an established room, rather than claiming that every part of the plan can serve every activity.

The teachers’ lounge is a smaller setting for preparation, pause and conversation. Together with the corridor seating, it extends the commission beyond the scheduled lesson. The design balances these shared uses with clear circulation, equipment integration and the need for teaching rooms to operate without unnecessary disturbance.

first-teaching-building.note: Commissioned project · Design stage shown: 30 January 2026. The documented scope is the 682 m² third-floor proposal; the page does not present a completed whole-building renovation.

rising-tides.intro: Rising Tides, Resilient Lives organises a public spine beneath the Ciliwung River viaduct at Kampung Melayu. Workshops, markets, kitchens, shared rooms, wetland edges and modular dwellings form a connected architectural system. Its principal design operation is sectional: everyday activity occupies a shaded civic landscape, while elevated access and adaptable rooms support a different pattern of use during inundation. The proposal uses the viaduct as a spatial reference; connections to transport infrastructure and structural feasibility are not assumed.

01: The two sections keep the main architectural frame comparable while changing the relation between water, circulation and programme. In ordinary conditions, the shared spaces support exchange, food preparation and work. In the flood scenario, access shifts toward elevated routes and boat landings, while parts of the civic programme accommodate refuge and relief.

This is a design for connected services rather than a collection of independently raised objects. A refuge needs a route to supplies and sanitation; a landing needs a clear relationship to occupied rooms. The comparison below makes those adjacencies visible. It is a spatial scenario, not a simulation of a verified flood level or a completed emergency operating plan.
02: Wetland buffers and water-related infrastructure are placed beside daily civic uses. Roof-water collection, wastewater treatment and overflow are read as distinct parts of the proposed system. Their separation matters: the presence of planted treatment space does not establish that floodwater is clean or that every flow can be reused.

The landscape helps organise edges between occupation and changing water. The design draws circulation, communal rooms and environmental systems together so their conflicts can be examined. Treatment capacity, water quality, debris, service isolation and safe levels remain subjects for engineering development.
03: The exploded dwelling study separates the frame, enclosure, ventilation and environmental components. Prefabrication is proposed as a way to make assembly legible and components replaceable. Community consultation and cooperative construction belong to the intended delivery approach; the unbuilt proposal does not establish that these processes have occurred.

At the larger scale, repetition allows individual units to relate to the shared spine. The architectural emphasis is on the connection between a dwelling and collective access, rather than the unit in isolation. Material availability, repair skills, procurement and the allocation of maintenance responsibilities would determine how this assembly strategy could be realised.

rising-tides.note: The companion research tests adaptation, unequal capacity and recovery after flooding. This project page concentrates on the selected spatial response: seasonal sections, programme relationships and a modular assembly system.

theater-design.intro: The Condenser gives a theatre two connected lives: enclosed rooms for performance and a more loosely occupied civic interior. Located among Wudaokou’s university, workplace and residential settings, it receives public approaches from the southwest and northwest, opens the ground, and carries shared space upward through foyers and stairs to a rooftop garden and amphitheatre. The blue and orange performance volumes remain identifiable within a translucent envelope. The project is an unbuilt academic proposal developed in spring 2025.

01: The ground is opened to support passage and arrival from two principal directions. At the southwest corner, a cut in the volume and a reflective surface give the entrance a distinct presence. The approach is intended to work as part of the surrounding pedestrian setting, with places to pause before entering the performance sequence.

The long section shows how the public ground relates to enclosed halls and upper shared spaces. The proposal concentrates performance in recognisable volumes and uses the spaces between them to extend occupation. Audience movement and backstage/loading access remain differentiated, allowing the public character of the building to be developed without assuming that its working areas are unrestricted.
02: Stairs are the main device connecting the civic interior. Landings and foyers become places for waiting, conversation and informal viewing. Between levels three and four, the larger gathering stair is conceived as a forum for talks, screenings and unscheduled occupation. Its scale distinguishes it from stairs used primarily for movement.

The design places opportunities to stay alongside the route through the building. This creates a sequence of changing pace rather than a single foyer emptied into the auditorium. The next technical stage would have to maintain accessible parallel routes, clear egress and acoustic separation when gathering and movement occur at the same time.
03: The blue western theatre and orange southern theatre respond to the different urban conditions around the site. A translucent polycarbonate envelope allows their interior light and occupation to register after dark. Colour differentiates the performance rooms within a common architectural frame; it does not replace the need for legible entrances and boundaries.

At roof level, the garden and open-air amphitheatre extend the range of settings for performance and gathering. The programme axonometric clarifies how these spaces relate to the enclosed rooms and backstage system below. The design is evaluated through these relationships, while opening hours, staffing, weather protection, acoustic performance and technical stage requirements remain part of further development.

theater-design.note: The research essay, Before the Curtain Rises, examines the institution’s non-performance hours through a comparative reading of OMA. This page presents Hao Chang’s own design decisions, drawings and proposed spatial sequence.

erdai.intro: The Erdai Art Museum places a collection of art within the inherited ground of the Dashan battery on the Fenggui Peninsula. Arrival begins at the former support area; a partly buried gallery sequence connects courts, adapted emplacement spaces and a tunnel toward the southern sea view. The museum follows the terrain instead of assembling every activity in a freestanding object. Its design works through differences of light, enclosure and outlook while retaining the distinction between surviving military fabric and new intervention.

01: Existing support spaces, trenches and artillery positions organise the visitor route. The former support area becomes an arrival and ticketing point, while selected emplacement spaces are adapted for outdoor sculpture. New galleries occupy a different relationship to the ground, connecting inherited elements without reconstructing a seamless military complex.

The layout is also a curatorial sequence. Ink, photography, ceramics, calligraphy and other works encounter different depths of daylight and different views. Courts provide orientation toward the battery and admit indirect light; the later tunnel and coastal room return the visitor to the horizon. The historic investigation and conservation report inform the site reading, while these spatial and curatorial choices belong to the proposal.

erdai.note: The sequence shown here is a design interpretation of the site and collection. Archaeology, structural condition, coastal drainage, object conservation and accessible circulation would need coordinated assessment before implementation.

spirited-a-way.intro: Spirited A Way proposes three forms of support along the Mount Kailash pilgrimage landscape: a courtyard lodge, a compact supply station and an interpretation hall set away from the ritual ground. They address different durations and needs of occupation. The design uses siting, thresholds and restrained material presence to differentiate shelter, replenishment and cultural interpretation, rather than repeating one building type along the route.

01: The route map links the three intervention types to their intended roles. The lodge supports a longer stay, the station addresses a shorter pause and replenishment, and the hall offers a separate setting for interpretation. The distribution is a design response to the research overlays; it is not a record of built or approved facilities.

Each intervention has a different relationship to approach and occupation. The lodge gathers rooms around a protected shared interior; the supply point is compact and legible from the route; the hall maintains distance from the ritual setting while framing a sheltered encounter with the landscape. Their programme and scale should be read together with the movements and services needed to support them.
C: The interpretation hall is placed away from the ritual ground rather than occupying it as a viewing platform. Stone, rammed earth and timber form the proposed material palette. Enclosure and openings organise a sequence between the landscape, prayer square and sheltered interior.

The design seeks a measured presence, but material restraint alone does not establish cultural or ecological suitability. The siting and programme would need to be reconsidered with custodians and users, alongside specialist assessment of hazards, servicing and maintenance. The architectural drawings show the proposed response and the questions it still has to satisfy.
A: The courtyard lodge works with the existing inn’s footprint. A new frame and insulated enclosure organise rooms around a sheltered common space, while the courtyard maintains an orientation toward the mountain’s north face. The design uses a known place of rest as its starting point rather than introducing an entirely separate destination.

The relationship between the room, covered threshold and courtyard offers different degrees of exposure. The shared interior supports rest and exchange after a demanding journey. Detailed thermal design, water supply, waste management and seasonal servicing would be developed with the people responsible for the facility.
B: The supply-station study combines compact rest and sanitation in prefabricated timber–aluminium modules. Elevated piles and an insulated enclosure are proposed to limit continuous ground contact and support a controlled interior within an exposed setting.

The compact plan concentrates functions instead of expanding them into a larger lodge. Its viability depends on delivery, servicing and waste removal as much as assembly. The project presents the module as a design hypothesis; logistics, environmental systems and site-specific foundation performance require further testing.

spirited-a-way.note: Research establishes the criteria for whether, where and how much to build. The project presents the particular lodge, station and hall designed to test those criteria; no cultural acceptance or environmental performance is inferred from the renderings.

books-above-bustles.intro: Books Above Bustles arranges library and shared civic programmes in suspended volumes between Chang’an Avenue and the hutongs. Gardens, bridges and reading spaces connect the volumes while the ground remains available for a more permeable relationship with the city. A mega-truss and modular timber grid organise the structural proposition. The section brings this support together with movement, programme and environmental systems so their relationships can be read within one architectural composition.

01: The sectional perspective is presented through four readings. Space locates the public routes and places to remain; structure identifies the supporting framework; climate places the proposed envelope, roof and ventilation systems; programme distinguishes reading, learning, work and shared rooms. The coloured overlays are interpretive guides to the drawing, not technical simulation outputs.

The design concentrates on connections between these systems. Bridges relate occupied volumes, gardens introduce another scale of shared interior, and the ground provides a civic setting beneath the institution. These relationships give the library a vertical public sequence while leaving questions of acoustic separation, servicing and accessible routes for detailed testing.
02: Suspension makes the ground a central architectural decision. The building’s mass is held above a more open pedestrian landscape, changing how the large avenue and smaller urban fabric can meet. The elevation and reflected surroundings give the volumes an urban presence, while the spaces beneath and between them carry the public-space proposition.

That ground should be read as part of an operating institution. The design provides a spatial framework for permeability; opening hours, entry control, maintenance and security would determine its realised public role. The project does not assume that visual transparency alone establishes unrestricted access.
03: Physical models study the proximity of the volumes, the depth of openings and the continuity of the supporting frame. They provide a second way to examine what can be difficult to read in a complex sectional perspective: where light enters, how voids align and how the mass is experienced from below.

The models are spatial studies. Long-span structural behaviour, deflection, connections, fire strategy and environmental performance require separate technical development. Their contribution at this stage is to make the relationship between built volume and shared void open to comparison and revision.

books-above-bustles.note: The Public Floor, the related research essay, examines thresholds, access and the institutional meaning of common ground. Here, the emphasis is the proposed massing, structural order, sectional connections and model studies.

teaching-building.intro: The first-prize atrium proposal for the Ziqiang Technology Building extends learning into the space between classrooms. Flexible seating, shared surfaces and planted areas turn circulation into a setting for short work sessions, conversation and gathering. The intervention is conceived as a connected interior landscape within the existing building, with different degrees of exposure and occupation around the common space.

01: The plan distinguishes movement through the atrium from places to stay along it. Shared surfaces support work and conversation; seating gives the circulation space destinations without assigning the whole interior to a single organised activity. Planting helps articulate smaller settings within the larger volume.

The spatial model tests how these elements relate across the atrium. The design seeks a balance between a recognisable common centre and places that can be occupied by individuals or small groups. Its flexibility lies in allowing several everyday uses within a defined spatial order, rather than leaving an empty floor with no guidance for occupation.

The proposal received first prize in the atrium design competition. It is distinct from the later commissioned First Teaching Building renewal. The drawings shown here document the competition scheme; acoustic performance, furniture specification, clear circulation and maintenance of planted areas would be resolved in subsequent design stages.

teaching-building.note: Competition proposal · 1st Prize. This page presents the atrium design as a separate work, with its own authorship and scope.

their-story.intro: Their Story translates an Eastern District community enquiry into a printed calendar. Its design medium is the edited sequence: local stories and images enter an object encountered repeatedly through the year. The project extends architectural attention to cultural representation—how a neighbourhood is described, remembered and made available to shared attention.

extra.title: The calendar as a repeated encounter
paragraphs: A calendar is read differently from an exhibition catalogue. It remains in an everyday setting and is returned to over time. The project uses that duration to give community stories a recurring presence, rather than treating them as material for a single event.

The design output brings research into a finite editorial form. Selection, ordering and the relationship between image and text become the principal decisions. The page presents that cultural object and its context without claiming that it represents every resident or resolves the neighbourhood’s differing interests.

extra.title: A scale between the personal and the district
paragraphs: The project keeps the scale of individual experience in view within a larger account of Eastern District. Its connection to architecture lies in attention to the people and practices through which a place acquires meaning, as well as the buildings through which it is usually identified.

The accompanying Hong Kong essay develops the wider questions about developers, cultural institutions and stewardship. The calendar remains a distinct output: an act of editing and circulation through which specific stories can be encountered.

their-story.note: Eastern District Community Calendar Project · Field research sponsored by Swire Properties · August–December 2024.

selected-studies.intro: Drawing, photography, graphic design and performance form a parallel practice of making and observation. The works below are organised through their media and roles: images composed on a page, space recorded through a lens, and movement developed with performers. Together they show other ways of working with attention, sequence, material and collective occupation.
selected-studies.note: Individual works and collaborative roles are identified in their captions. This collection remains the final entry in the chronological portfolio.

waterfront-plus.intro: Waterfront+ reconnects the Shichahai water edge with the depth of its lanes, courtyards and shared spaces. The proposal works across Yandai Xiejie, Di’anmen, the Fire God Temple and Baimi Xiejie through selected passages, courtyard adaptation, public programmes and landscape adjustments. It retains differentiated residential thresholds rather than opening every edge uniformly. The project received the 2025 China Human Settlements Academic Year Award, Gold Award in Urban Design.

01: The overall plan links interventions at the scale of the node, the route and the district. Existing landmarks provide orientation, but the design also addresses the smaller connections that make the waterfront part of ordinary neighbourhood movement. Selected openings and adjusted circulation connect the lake with spaces behind the commercial edge.

Before-and-after drawings distinguish retained elements, adapted structures and new relationships. The strategy does not depend on a continuous new waterfront object. It assembles a sequence in which public landscape, shared facilities and commercial interfaces each have a different role, with domestic areas maintaining their own degree of enclosure.
02: The courtyard is the main unit of incremental change. Plans and sections test how shared use can be introduced while retaining the scale and depth of the inherited fabric. The proposed community library, activity centre and shared dining give the connected route destinations beyond visitor consumption.

The waterfront section makes the relationship between water-facing activity and the neighbourhood legible. Changes in level, entry and enclosure differentiate public passage from domestic occupation. This is an urban-design proposal; ownership, resident agreements, conservation review and the operation of new shared facilities remain necessary to develop it into an implementation programme.

waterfront-plus.note: Research asks who benefits from greater permeability and how residential continuity can be protected. The project shows the selected spatial interventions through its overall plan, before-and-after studies, courtyards and sections.
